articles.title_orig: Trump says he has rejected Iranian proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Trump says he has rejected Iranian proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, after Iranian officials indicated that shipping through the critical waterway could resume within days if a deal was sealed.
“I rejected their deal. They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump told reporters as he boarded Marine One on the White House lawn, after indirect talks between the two countries were held on the sidelines of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York.
“What they wanted is to immediately open the Hormuz Strait. You know why? Because they’re dying. You know why they’re dying? Because they have no money coming in because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait,” he continued. “They outsmarted themselves. They said, ‘Let’s close it and cause a problem for the world.’ And I came along, and we put up the greatest blockade ever in military history.”
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected Iran’s offer to revive a ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz .
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had said Friday that the choice “rests with the United States.”
“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi told reporters.
He said a “concrete seven-day plan” that includes reopening the strait had been conveyed to the U.S. through mediator Qatar and was ready to start “as soon as the United States accepts this plan.”
Iran offers new proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
Araghchi said the actions required of the U.S. in Iran’s proposal were commitments already agreed to in the June memorandum of understanding between the two countries that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire. That agreement, signed in June, collapsed within days after fresh strikes were exchanged.
One of the conditions of the plan is for the U.S. to accept a maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz that has been agreed upon by Iran and Oman , Araghchi had said Thursday.
A U.S. official said on Friday that the Trump administration was having positive and constructive discussions through the mediators but that it was not in any hurry to reach an agreement.
“The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush,” the U.S. official said. “Over the last 48 hours, nearly 40 million barrels of oil have transited the strait.”
Earlier this week, Trump said he was still considering whether to “annihilate” Iran or make a deal. Early Saturday, he posted an image to Truth Social of the Strait of Hormuz labeled the “Trump Strait.”
In an interview with Al Jazeera on Saturday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that resolving the Hormuz issue “is possible through negotiations, not the use of force,” but warned that his country does not “trust” talks with Washington.
Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon. Soon after the war started, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy.
Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November.
“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said in a brief meeting with NBC News and other news organizations, two days after Trump said he believed the Iranian regime would not make a deal to settle the conflict until after the elections .
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
Polls show Democrats with an advantage heading into the November midterms. The latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 31% of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, while 69% disapproved.
The U.S. this week announced it would impose sanctions on any global companies doing business ​with Iranian airlines, with the aim of grounding Iran’s entire civil fleet worldwide.
Iraq said Saturday that it was engaging with the U.S. in an effort to restore humanitarian flights to and from Iran, after Iranian airlines were barred from neighboring countries in response to the sanctions.
Efforts were ongoing to “secure exemptions for certain Iraqi airports from these measures” in order to enable “the resumption of flights for humanitarian reasons, such as medical treatment, education, religious pilgrimages, and the interests of civilians,” the Iraqi prime minister’s office said.
Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that flights had also been shut down to Oman, Georgia and Azerbaijan.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Philadelphia region braces for nor’easter: N.J. and Del. see high waves, coastal flooding
articles.title_zh: Philadelphia region braces for nor’easter: N.J. and Del. see high waves, coastal flooding
articles.content_orig:
New York and New Jersey issued a state of emergency as the storm struck.
The early-season nor’easter hit the East Coast Saturday bringing in torrential rain, high winds and flood warnings for millions of people.
Streets in New Jersey and New York, which were under a state of emergency, were already flooded as the storm and high tide combined for dangerous conditions. Waves of 16 feet or more have been reported by buoys off the Jersey Shore and southern New England.
Late Friday night, a weather station in Surf City, New Jersey, reported a wind gust of 74 mph. Other stations along the Jersey Shore have reported wind gusts of 60 mph or more.
The winds toppled trees in New York City, with some landing on top of parked cars.
Tidal flood waters peaked at moderate flood stage late Friday rose ahead of high tide later Saturday morning.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who already declared a state of emergency, told reporters Saturday morning that much more rain was coming.
"With tonight's full moon, the tides may even be higher. We expect waves as tall as 20 feet in some areas. Winds will be just as powerful as the waves, wind gusts exceeding 50, even 60 miles an hour, have already been recorded on Long Island," she said at a news conference.
The governor added that power outages were expected throughout the state and warned residents to be prepared.
Subways and trains have been operating as expected so far, according to the governor. Storm doors have been added at rail yards at Coney Island and Howard Beach to reduce the chance of impacts on service, Hochul said.
"Here's the bottom line: Stay out of the water. Although we just saw a surfer on one of the cameras off the coast of Long Island, stay out of the water," she said. "Anyone who goes in or near the water this weekend is literally gambling with their life."
Parts of the southern Chesapeake Bay to the Jersey Shore and into the Raritan Bay reached moderate to major flood stage from coastal flooding during high tide Saturday morning. While the tide has begun to recede, some of these areas mentioned are still dealing with moderate to major coastal flooding.
Coastal flood alerts remain in effect from eastern Virginia through southern Maine, including Virginia Beach, Philadelphia, New York City, New London, Connecticut, Providence, Rhode Island, and Boston.
Moderate to major coastal flooding is possible during high tide later Saturday evening from the southern Chesapeake Bay to the Jersey Shore and up to Raritan Bay.
Wind advisories remain in effect from the Delmarva Peninsula up to eastern Massachusetts, including Dover, Delaware; Philadelphia; New York City; Hartford, Connecticut; and Worcester, Massachusetts, for winds gusting up to 45 mph.
High wind warnings are in effect for the Jersey Shore, as well as parts of Rhode Island and Massachusetts, including Boston, Providence and Atlantic City, for winds gusting up to 60 mph. The winds can knock down trees and power lines.
High waves of 6 to 12 feet or more will continue to pound the coastline from coastal Delmarva through the Jersey Shore, Long Island and southeastern coastal New England, producing widespread and potentially significant beach erosion and dangerous coastal conditions.
Per police in Stafford Township, New Jersey, the Route 72 causeway into Long Beach Island has been closed to non-essential personnel.
According to the National Weather Service, evacuations were underway for hotels in the vicinity along Black Horse Pike in New Jersey earlier this morning. Parts of the Black Horse Pike are underwater in multiple places, resulting in the closure of the roadway.
On Saturday afternoon and evening, rounds of heavy rain and strong wind gusts will continue from Maryland to southern New York and begin stretching into southern New England. High tide around 9 p.m. could produce moderate coastal flooding, with some isolated major coastal flooding possible.
Overnight into Sunday morning, rounds of heavy rain and strong wind gusts will continue from Maryland to southern New England as several rounds of heavy rain will move through before sunrise, with isolated instances of inland flash flooding possible.
The nor’easter will continue to linger on Sunday but begin to break up and weaken. Winds and rain will begin to lighten, though gusty winds and some heavier pockets of rain will remain possible with potential lingering impacts into Monday.
Rainfall totals will be widespread at 2 to 4 inches across the Northeast, with some of the highest totals reaching up to 6 inches from New Jersey to Boston.
Some inland flash flooding will be possible, especially in areas with poor drainage, where blown leaves can clog storm drains, or where the heaviest bands of rain move through.
However, because the rain is falling over such a long duration, inland flash flooding will not be the most widespread threat as wind-driven rain could instead lead to power outages.

articles.title_orig: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
articles.title_zh: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
articles.content_orig:
Kirk's Utah Valley University event was held in a courtyard surrounded by tall buildings
An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.
The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA.
It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers.
The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025.
Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed.
University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report , external - published by UVU - says.
"But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds.
Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note.
They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team.
A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said.
The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures.
However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety.
Charlie Kirk was addressing about 3,000 people when he was shot in the neck
Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice , a step that can precede legal action.
The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones.
"The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."
When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement.
The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events.
UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations".
It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures now common practice at high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors.
Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead.
His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.

articles.title_orig: Rogue OpenAI agents targeted three separate US government websites
articles.title_zh: Rogue OpenAI agents targeted three separate US government websites
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI has been at the centre of new concerns over uncontrolled AI activity
OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly.
AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said.
The disclosures come days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme.
Since August, public fears have grown over the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control.
OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information".
But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites.
When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said.
OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public.
However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended.
In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have.
Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.
The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data.
Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data."
It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.
Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog.
In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites.
In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended.
OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details.
"Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said.
Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted.
"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address."
Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?
Could AI wipe out humans and how might it do it?
The company said many of the incidents are being referred to as "agent spam", which it described as "unexpected or concerning" AI agent activity, like posting information to the internet.
OpenAI began taking such incidents more seriously after an incident in July where a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face without being prompted to do so.
Hugging Face was first to go public with the incident, with OpenAI publicly taking responsibility for it later.
Clement Delangue, the head of Hugging Face, during a United Nations Security Council session on AI on Wednesday: "I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly."
"Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring," Delangue added.
During that same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the head of rival firm Anthropic, asked for international leaders to form global standards for AI safety and ways to monitor and report such incidents.
Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack
While OpenAI and Anthropic have both said in recent weeks that they will bring third-party evaluators inside their companies to do real-time safety evaluations of AI tools and models, such evaluators have not yet arrived, as the BBC has reported .
OpenAI said on Friday that it is currently reviewing training activity by its AI agents and going back on a "month by month" basis from when the Hugging Face hack occurred.
"Most cases identified so far have been low severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact," the company said. "Given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete."
David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at University of Montreal and the founder of AI safety group Evitable, said on Friday that he was "deeply troubled" by the increasing number of AI-related safety incidents.
He called for "an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium" on AI development.
"We have yet to understand the extent of existing incidents, and future rogue AI scenarios could be catastrophic," Krueger said.

articles.title_orig: Body of 10th woman found in South Africa as killings investigation continues
articles.title_zh: Body of 10th woman found in South Africa as killings investigation continues
articles.content_orig:
South African police said Saturday that another woman's body had been found near Johannesburg, bringing the number of victims to 10 in a series of killings under investigation.
Police began investigating after the bodies of three women were found in July and August within about 4.3 miles of one another in the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg.
The discovery of six bodies in Ekurhuleni over 10 days earlier this month raised fears that a serial killer or killers were responsible.
Two women were arrested and charged last week with murder in relation to the ninth body , discovered on Sept. 17. The victim had been stabbed and had her throat cut, police said. Police did not link the two women charged to any of the other killings.
Provincial police commissioner Lt. Gen. Tommy Mthombeni told state broadcaster SABC on Saturday that investigators believed the ninth killing was an isolated case but could not rule out the possibility that some of the other cases were linked.
Police had issued a warning for women to use caution while in the area.
Police have identified similarities in some of the killings but said they had not found conclusive evidence that the same person or people were responsible.
All nine of the bodies discovered before Saturday were those of women in their 20s or 30s, according to police. Several were naked or partially clothed and left in open areas near main roads. Officers from the Investigative Psychology Unit, which specializes in complex or serial violent crimes, are part of the investigation.
Police released limited details about the 10th body, which was found early Saturday, and did not immediately identify the victim.
"We can only confirm the discovery of the body," the South African Police Service said in a statement. "Crime scene management and all the necessary role players are currently on the scene."
South Africa has high rates of violent crime and violence against women. Three women were killed every day by an intimate partner from 2020-2021, a recent study found.
The country has one of the highest global murder rates , with more than 60 a day on average.
The killings in Ekurhuleni have sparked a national outcry over women's safety.

articles.title_orig: Azerbaijan Grand Prix: Russell holds off Verstappen in super-close finish, Norris crashes out - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: Azerbaijan Grand Prix: Russell holds off Verstappen in super-close finish, Norris crashes out - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend went the way many believed the 2026 season would play out. George Russell strolled to victory from pole, though with a little late jeopardy, whilst Kimi Antonelli ’s crash in qualifying meant he had to fight his way through the field to finish fifth. That, after all, was the order of things last season.
Yet the past few days in Baku are an inversion of the season’s storyline. It is Antonelli who has been the faster driver, heading for a maiden world title at the second time of asking. Russell has been the troubled one. This was only the Briton’s third victory of the season and his first since Austria in late June. Antonelli has racked up eight wins and, before this weekend in Baku, a well-deserved 81-point lead over Russell.
Russell’s dominant and impressive run from pole to the chequered flag on Saturday is both a reminder of what he is capable of and also what might have been, had he been able to find this type of form earlier and more often. The reality, though, is that he needs to replicate this for the rest of the season to even be in with a sniff, barring a catastrophic meltdown from Antonelli. Still, Russell looked elated to have ended his barren run.
The finish was a little more tense than Russell deserved, having established a healthy lead in the first half of the race. Two late safety cars eradicated his advantage and helped put Max Verstappen’s Red Bull on his gearbox. In the end, he triumphed by just under 0.2sec and, as Antonelli finished fifth – with some help from two safety-car inducing crashes – he made up 15 points on his Mercedes team-mate. Isack Hadjar completed the podium for Red Bull after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.
A drag race to the finish line! 🍿 #F1 #AzerbaijanGP pic.twitter.com/Nb6xfkkpIb
Whether or not this performance is too little from Russell, it is almost certainly too late . The margin to the championship leader is now down to 66 points with a probable seven rounds – including one sprint race – remaining. It improves Russell’s chances of a championship from “unthinkable” to “remote”.
Russell has already written off his own hopes of beating Antonelli to the championship. He did not seem to have changed his mind or his approach after stepping out of his car victoriously.
“Win every race. That’s the game plan,” Russell said. “My team-mate’s had an incredible season, he’s been pretty flawless throughout, but now we’re getting to crunch time.
“I’m just going to focus on myself. If I continue giving performances like I did this weekend, at the end of the season I’ll be happy because it’s been a tough period for me and I’ll feel like I’ve come through the other side.”
In fairness to Russell, his eighth grand prix victory did not come entirely out of nowhere as he has been much closer to Antonelli since the summer break. With a bit more luck in Zandvoort and Monza, he may have been closer still.
“I think it’s just having more experience with this new driving style I’ve adopted and every race since the break I feel like I’ve gone from strength to strength. I feel more like myself again,” he added.
Russell would have had an easier route to victory were it not for the two safety car periods in the second half of the race. The first came out after Alexander Albon slammed his Williams into the barriers at turn five on lap 31 of 51. That bunched the pack up and wiped out the 10-second lead that Russell had built up over Oscar Piastri’s McLaren.
As is so often the case in F1, and especially on street circuits, one safety car often brings about another. And so it was as Franco Colapinto’s enormously optimistic divebomb up the inside of turn one on the lap-36 restart took out not only his Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly, but also McLaren’s Lando Norris.
Absolute chaos at the restart 😵 #F1 #AzerbaijanGP pic.twitter.com/o4Q5MdHLnc
Norris had stern words for Colapinto, who has been handed a five-place grid drop for the next race in Malaysia, after his elimination. “There’s just some drivers that shouldn’t be in Formula One, to be honest,” the reigning world champion said.
“I think the FIA should start handing out bans for this kind of stuff. It’s careless, it costs a lot of money. All my parts are in the bin,” he added.
The greatest pressure Russell faced came after the second restart, after Verstappen moved swiftly into second. The Dutchman, who has yet to win in 2026, is not a driver anybody wants to see fill their mirrors at the best of times, let alone when trying to end a 12-week, six-race win drought.
Yet Verstappen could not find a way past. The most threatening moment of the final 12 laps was on the final push to the chequered flag. Valtteri Bottas put his Cadillac in the wall, bringing out double-waved yellow flags at turn 15. Russell lost his electrical boost on the run to the line but managed to hold off Verstappen by just 0.196sec, the closest winning margin for more than two decades.
As for Antonelli? He surely just needs to keep his car out of the wall, whatever Russell does.

articles.title_zh: White House blocks CNN from traveling with Trump on Air Force One
articles.content_orig:
CNN had been scheduled to fly with Trump on Air Force One
Broadcaster CNN has been barred from travelling with US President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee on Saturday.
The move is the latest in a battle between the White House and the media after it was forced to lift its ban on some news outlets.
CNN was scheduled to fly with Trump for his trip to Tennessee for a college American football game until a note released on Friday night by the White House did not list the broadcaster on the media schedule.
The BBC has requested comment from the White House.
CNN has reported that no other outlet was listed as replacing them in the president's tentative schedule.
Last week, Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists from the White House after accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.
All three media outlets said they were pursuing legal action and accused Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.
Four television networks that have a daily rotation of White House coverage alongside CNN - ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - had paused their broadcasts of the president in solidarity with the banned outlets.
The White House then launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York.
A federal judge has since ruled that Trump barring news outlets from the White House was likely unconstitutional and that the administration had to let them back in, at least for now.
However, the White House still denied entry to some CNN and MS NOW reporters assigned to cover arrivals at a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday.
A White House communications account earlier posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event and every press call".
Regular US television coverage resumed on Friday after White House officials allowed reporters entry.
The president is set to attend a football game between University of Tennessee vs University of Texas College at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville from midday local time on Saturday.

articles.title_orig: Third suspect arrested in death of Mississippi woman found hanging at ‘staged’ crime scene
articles.title_zh: Third suspect arrested in death of Mississippi woman found hanging at ‘staged’ crime scene
articles.content_orig:
Warning: This story contains distressing details
Police in the US state of Mississippi have said they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" by being placed hanging in a tree.
The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs.
The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.
Police said that the medical examiner had determined that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".
Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging may have been staged.
Fortune's mother told the BBC that she remembered the coroner telling her: "We're not treating this as [an] actual hanging." Her daughter, they told her, was dead before being placed in the tree.
Christy Spivey also recalled police telling her the incident was "drug related".
She described how she knew her daughter fought for her life till the very end while speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday.
"I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey said, adding that Fortune had left behind four young children, aged seven, five, four and one.
Dressed in a shirt that read "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she did not want to see any innocent people going to jail.
"I just hope they have the right people," she said.
Three people have so far been arrested in relation to the case, all of whom are black, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody without bail.
A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in relation to the case this week.
A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday.
The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.
Representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, cited at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress , external , which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.
The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has since been ruled a suicide.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.content_orig:
NAALEHU, Hawaii — Hurricane Nolo is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane in the Pacific Ocean over the weekend and unleash intense rain, the possibility of life-threatening flash flooding and dangerous surf for Hawaii’s Big Island.
Nolo was a Category 5 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 160 mph early Saturday, the National Hurricane Center said, as its outer rainbands hit the Big Island. Hurricane conditions are possible on the island, especially in areas with steep terrain, the weather service warned.
The storm was moving north-northwest at 10 mph on Saturday morning, but was expected to turn northeast and head toward Baja California Sur on Monday.
This marks the third hurricane in less than two months to whip past Hawaii (following Lala and Lowell ). The active Pacific hurricane season is likely due to a record-setting El Niño — a natural climate pattern characterized by a rise in sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific, which can spawn more intense and frequent cyclones there.
Tess Kala, a South Point resident who grew up in the area, said the back-to-back storms are a shock to locals.
“Honestly, this is the first like, whoa, what happened? We had a lot of family and friends that have lived here all their lives through generations and never experienced this before,” she said.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said Friday that President Donald Trump approved the state’s request for an emergency declaration to provide federal assistance for emergency protective measures across the state.
Mark Peters, a resident of seven years of Naalehu, on the Big Island’s southern tip, said the damage from the recent hurricanes has not been forgotten.
“It hurts me when I see friends and neighbors and people of this community that I know, and I just see it in their eyes, I hear it in their voices. We’ve been through a lot down here, and we still got a lot to go,” Peters said.
“We’re just getting started with our recovery. But to have yet another big storm hit us, and potentially even bigger than the last one, it’s difficult,” he said.
While he praised his community for its resilience, he said the people are still in need of basics like food and water, and many are in the process of reconstruction.
“We’re talking years. This is going to be a long recovery,” Peters said Friday.
He recalled driving through Waiohinu in the aftermath of Hurricane Lala and his “eyes getting wide open with all the damage, and the cars and houses moved and not where they’re supposed to be, and Waiohinu Park having buildings in the baseball field.”
Kala, the South Point resident, is preparing for Nolo by “moving everything away from the houses, tying things down, making sure that everything is hosed up and taped up as best as we possibly can.”
Nolo will bring periods of heavy rain that will continue across the Big Island and Maui over the weekend, and could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain across eastern and southern portions of both the Big Island and Maui, the hurricane center said.
Nolo is forecast to dump 8 to 12 inches of rain on the eastern and southern parts of the Big Island, with maximum amounts up to 16 inches. Western portions of the Big Island could see 1 to 3 inches of rain, with maximum amounts of 6 inches. Meanwhile, Maui could see 4 to 6 inches, with maximum amounts of 8 inches, the National Hurricane Center said.
The rest of Hawaii will experience smaller rainfall totals, but isolated flooding is possible.
Nolo could also bring large and damaging waves along portions of the Big Island’s coastline into the weekend.
A hurricane watch and tropical storm warning are in effect for Hawaii County, and a tropical storm watch is in effect for Maui County. A hurricane watch means that hurricane conditions are possible within 24-36 hours. A wind advisory has been issued for the rest of the state.
Tropical storm-force winds will reach the Big Island on Friday afternoon, with hurricane-force winds possible by late evening.
A high surf advisory is in effect for the south- and east-facing shores of the Big Island and the east-facing shores of Maui and Molokai. A high-surf advisory was also issued for the east-facing shores of Niihau, Kauai and Oahu beginning Friday evening.
Nolo could also spawn tornadoes and large waterspouts over and near the Big Island and to the right of the track of the tropical cyclone.
Marlene Lenthang reported from Los Angeles, and Ryan Chandler and Shanshan Dong reported from Naalehu, Hawaii.

High-stakes discussions on trade and artificial intelligence unfold in New York City as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer meet with Chinese officials. Fox News contributor Dan Hoffman analyzes this strategic framework between the world's two most powerful nations ahead of the upcoming summit with President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
The United States and China agreed to lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods traded between the two countries following a three-day summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C.
According to the White House, the $30 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions apply to "non-sensitive goods."
U.S. exports including agricultural products, fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics and medical devices will receive favorable tariff treatment in China. Meanwhile, U.S. imports of Chinese-made small appliances, toys, holiday decorations and children's car seats will also receive preferential treatment.
The agreement was reached through the U.S.-China Board of Trade, a body first proposed during Trump's visit to China in May and formally established during Xi's visit to Washington this week.
President Donald Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping to speak during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House on Sept. 24, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
XI PRAISES US STATE VISIT 'PERFECTION' AS TRUMP CALLS MEETINGS 'VERY PRODUCTIVE'
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that "a lot more details" about the new trade agreement will be released on Monday.
Greer said the tariff terms were hammered out after weeks of negotiations. Neither country has released the final tariff rates or all the products that will receive favored status going forward.
This marks one of the most significant cooldowns in the trade war Trump launched against China in February 2025, when he levied a 10% tariff on all Chinese imports, citing Beijing's alleged role in the fentanyl crisis and illegal immigration. China hit back with levies on U.S. coal, liquefied natural gas, crude oil and cars.
President Donald Trump holds up a tariff chart while speaking during a "Make America Wealthy Again" trade announcement event in the Rose Garden at the White House on April 2, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
BESSENT REVEALS EXTENSION TO BUSAN AGREEMENT WITH CHINA UNTIL JANUARY
At their peak, U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods reached a staggering 145% in April 2025, shortly after Trump unveiled his "Liberation Day" reciprocal tariffs. China responded with tariffs of up to 125% on U.S. goods.
U.S. and Chinese negotiators met in Geneva in May 2025 and agreed to a 90-day truce that lowered U.S. tariffs to 30% and China's to 10%. The agreement was extended for another 90 days in August.
President Donald Trump walks on a red carpet after greeting Chinese President Xi Jinping during an arrival ceremony on Sept. 23, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Trump and Xi reached another tentative agreement during talks in South Korea in October 2025. Under the deal, China agreed to crack down on fentanyl precursors, resume purchases of U.S. soybeans and ease restrictions on rare-earth exports , while the United States agreed to further ease tariffs.
The two countries will now use the Board of Trade to negotiate additional tariff reductions and other trade disputes, leaving open the possibility of broader agreements in the months ahead.

articles.title_orig: Chevy's New V8: Why Cars Will Have Engine Oil Dipsticks But Trucks Won't
articles.title_zh: Chevy's New V8: Why Cars Will Have Engine Oil Dipsticks But Trucks Won't
articles.content_orig:
Among the oldest engines still in production today is the small-block Chevy (SBC) V8, and you may have heard that GM recently took the covers off the latest entrants into the sixth-gen family — the 5.7-liter L76 and 6.6-liter L78. While the headline figures of more power and capability are all exciting news, the fact that these engines no longer feature the good 'ol dipstick might come as a bit of a letdown to ardent GM fans.
Although GM is not the first company to drop dipsticks , many enthusiasts consider it an unnecessary complication to engine maintenance. However, that's not exactly the sentiment that Ian Stahl, Assistant Chief Engineer of Small Block Engines at GM, has towards the idea. Speaking to YouTube's The Fast Lane Truck , Stahl was quoted as saying, "I've never been a fan of them." He likens the whole oil dipstick shebang to how many people didn't like seatbelts back in the old days. "Now, nobody thinks twice about [seatbelts]... so everything takes time to get accustomed to," according to Stahl.
Perhaps his rationale of not many owners checking oil or knowing how to check it correctly may hold water, but apart from that, the engine's packaging and other design considerations also played their part in the decision to ditch the traditional setup. Instead, what you find is a battery of sensors that rely on a number of parameters, including driving time, temperature, and miles driven, to check the oil pressure, oil level, and oil life.
While the video's comment section didn't spare Stahl or his remarks, it's worth noting that these sixth-gen small blocks do bring along several noteworthy upgrades over the outgoing 5.3 and 6.2.
Before we get into the specifics, it's important to understand that these new 5.7 and 6.6 V8s aren't the first of the sixth-gen engines to arrive. That honor goes to the 2027 Corvette's 6.7-liter LS6 motor . What's interesting, however, is that, according to GM Authority , unlike the latest sixth-gen small blocks, the LS6 does feature an oil dipstick. Remember, these 5.7s and 6.6s are for the latest crop of GM light-duty trucks. When comparing the 6.7 LS6 to the 6.6 L78, engineers told Car and Driver that the LS6, in addition to its slightly larger displacement, had hardware changes that wouldn't have made sense for the trucks. Also, the LS6 is dry-sumped, so make of that what you will.
Dipstick controversy aside, the 5.7-liter L76 V8 puts out 402 horsepower and 428 pound-feet of torque, which is significantly more than the 5.3's 355 horses and 383 torques. As for the 6.6-liter L78, the V8 belts out 481 horsepower and 501 pound-feet of torque, numbers that make the outgoing 6.2's 420 hp and 460 lb-ft look a lot less impressive. Increasing the stroke length by 6 mm helped the engines make more power and torque, as did the use of larger throttle bodies, new intake manifolds, and increased compression ratios. The combination of port and direct fuel injection is another sixth-gen highlight, as well as the introduction of a new lubrication system.
While GM chose the unconventional route for its latest truck V8s, that's not the case with the 3.0-liter straight-6 Duramax diesel and 2.7-liter TurboMax inline-four. These engines continue with the traditional oil dipstick. And if it makes you feel any better, the Ram 1500's twin-turbo 3.0-liter inline-6 is also dipstick-free.

articles.title_orig: 4 American tourists dead after building explosion and collapse in Athens
articles.title_zh: 4 American tourists dead after building explosion and collapse in Athens
articles.content_orig:
Four Americans were among the six people who died after an explosion and building collapse in Athens' tourist district of Plaka near the Acropolis on Friday, officials said.
The blast, which occurred at dawn on Friday, was likely caused by a gas leak, according to Athens Mayor Haris Doukas.
The two other people killed were an elderly British man and his Greek wife who lived on the second floor of the three-story building, Greece's state broadcaster ERT reported.
The American family of four had been renting an apartment on the first floor and were preparing to go to the airport hours later Friday for their return to the United States when the blast occurred, according to the Kathimerini newspaper.
The explosion brought down the residential building and damaged properties and vehicles along the street. Two other women were injured from an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, fire brigades said, according to the Associated Press.
The New York Times reported that the U.S. family was composed of a couple, their son and his girlfriend. Greek authorities did not immediately give their identities, ages or where in the U.S. they came from.
On Saturday, AFP reporters saw mechanical diggers moving debris at the site and thermal-imaging cameras deployed.
"We are talking about an incredible disaster," Doukas said.
Two nearby buildings were left in a dangerous state, he added, with inspections underway "to determine if they can remain standing or if they also have to be demolished."
The owner of the ground-floor apartment, Mathaios Artavanis, told the Kathimerini daily he was absent at the time of the blast. He said he had tried afterward to contact the U.K.-Greek couple who lived there, without success.
Video footage from the scene showed rubble strewn across the street, with parked cars smashed by falling debris. The people rescued by the fire department from the adjacent building were all tourists, resident Andreas Martzaklis said.
The pastor of a nearby church said this Sunday's service would be held outdoors because of damage to the church.
A year ago, locals in the Plaka neighborhood had warned the city and utility companies about the risk of gas leaks or short circuits, according to a letter by the residents' association published by Kathimerini.
The residents had urged a fire drill to identify possible weaknesses in the emergency response plans for the district.
A citizens' group said on social media that one resident in the street where the explosion happened had alerted authorities after smelling a possible gas leak.
The neighborhood is one of Athens' most popular tourist areas. The nearby Acropolis, one of Greece's best-known landmarks, welcomed 4.6 million visitors last year.

articles.title_zh: Inside the ultra-luxury sober living home where Presley Gerber died of suspected overdose
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford who spoke eloquently about his struggles with addiction and mental health, entered the mansion-like sober living home in an elite section of Santa Monica on Saturday night.
The next morning, he was found dead of what police said was a drug overdose.
His death has brought much mourning as well as questions about how he could overdose on drugs while inside the  Resolution Living facility.
Santa Monica Police are investigating the source of the drugs he had taken, while the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner is awaiting toxicology results before making a finding on the cause of death. It comes amid growing scrutiny of the industry.
The Resolutions Living home operates in a regulatory gray area and is not authorized to provide medical care. There is no state agency in charge of monitoring or tracking the locations of sober living homes, which are protected under state and federal law as residences of people with disabilities. This situation has prompted calls for more regulations.
The California Department of Health Services is investigating whether Resolutions Living is providing any services that would require a state license after receiving a complaint about the sober living home Wednesday, according to department spokesperson Anthony Cava.
Beyond being the site of the death, it’s unclear what role the Resolutions Living facility plays in the investigation. The sober living home is owned by psychologist Reza Nabavi and his wife, clinical psychologist Maryam Akbar, who together purchased the property in the wealthy Northeast neighborhood of Santa Monica for $5.8 million in 2021.
Prior to entering the treatment industry, Nabavi struggled with substance use issues himself.
He was charged with felony drug possession after Oakland Police found him asleep in a car with a gun, meth and a 15-year-old girl in 2002 — an incident that later became a roadblock on his path to obtaining a psychology license.
He went on to work as director of family services at the now defunct Promises treatment center in Malibu from June 2006 to May 2011, according to his LinkedIn . In 2007, a Times investigation revealed that the celebrity rehab had been cited by state regulators for providing medical services outside the scope of its licenses and was facing four consumer protection lawsuits alleging predatory business practices . A search of lawsuits against Promises did not list Nabavi as a defendant, and there is no indication in public records that he was involved in those allegations.
Details are unclear on what safety practices were in place at the sober living home where Gerber died.
Resolutions Living is not subject to state regulatory oversight, because it operates as a recovery home and doesn’t offer treatment on site. The medical arm of Nabavi’s and Akbar’s treatment program, Resolutions Therapeutic Services, is housed in a separate facility down the street
Nabavi, 50, did not return several messages for comment and has not addressed his history, Gerber’s death or specifics about the sober living home.
Nabavi’s initial effort to become a psychologist was denied in 2004 by the California Psychology Board because of two prior misdemeanor convictions for drug possession.
In 2002, he was found in a car with five “zip lock baggies containing methamphetamine,” a .357-caliber handgun and a teenage girl who told police she was under the influence of narcotics, according to records referenced in a state psychology board ruling. He was arrested on Oakland’s 5th Street, a place the patrol officers described as known for “frequent narcotic and prostitution activity.”
Nabavi was charged with two counts of felony drug possession with a firearm. He pleaded no contest to the lesser charge of misdemeanor drug possession and was sentenced to 36 months’ probation.
About a month later, Oakland Police arrested him with methamphetamine and a glass pipe. After six days in jail, he again pleaded no contest to drug possession under Proposition 36, which allows people convicted of certain drug offenses to receive treatment in place of jail time.
The California Psychology Board approved Nabavi’s license in 2006, placing him on probationary registration for five years with requirements that he undergo substance use treatment and complete random drug testing.
In 2008, Nabavi convinced the state psychology board to end his probation early, saying that he had been clean and sober since May 2002, spent 80 hours that year in the Proposition 36 drug program and gotten a master’s degree and doctorate, and that his practice concentrated on drug and alcohol addiction.
In the hills of Malibu, a celebrity rehab center visited by stars such as Britney Spears and Charlie Sheen is hitting the market for $19.95 million.
Nabavi and Akhbar purchased the Resolutions Living home, which is valued today at $7.7 million, with seven bedrooms, nine bathrooms, a library and a movie theater in 2021. They then purchased a neighboring property at 1010 Berkeley St. for $4.45 million in 2022.
The couple operate Resolutions Therapeutic Services, a licensed mental health treatment facility, in a medical office building about a mile away.
In 2020, Nabavi was sued by a former Resolutions Therapeutic Services patient who alleged that he was denied $46,353 in insurance benefits as a result of the company’s negligence and was asked to pay the company more than $20,000 to cover the cost of urine tests. The plaintiff moved to dismiss the suit the following year and his attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment on why the suit was dropped or whether a settlement was reached outside court.
Repeated attempts to establish regulatory standards for sober-living homes have been unsuccessful. At least 25 bills affecting sober living homes were introduced in the state Legislature between 1998 and 2016, but none became law.
This legislative cycle,  Assemblymember Laurie Davies (R-Laguna Niguel) introduced Assembly Bill 423 , which would have required that business-operated recovery homes register with the State Department of Health Care Services. However, the proposal failed to advance in the legislature.
Davies said she was frustrated that the fairly straightforward bill, which would have enabled the state to track the number and location of recovery homes, did not gain traction.
“We can’t get an accurate count of how many recovery homes even exist in California,” she said. “And you cannot regulate what you can’t see.”
Part of the pushback to increased oversight probably likely stems from the fact that the Department of Health Care Services is understaffed, she said, pointing to the fact that it can take more than a year to investigate complaints about licensed substance use treatment facilities.
Pete Nielsen, president of California Consortium of Addiction Programs and Professionals, has advocated for creating a recovery home certification process in California.
“Today, there is still no statewide standard for what qualifies as a recovery residence, no consistent consumer protections for residents, and no objective framework for funding decisions,” he wrote in a blog post . “That vacuum has fueled controversy rather than solutions.”
Speaking generally, Nielsen supports using standards set by the National Alliance for Recovery Residences to create a California recovery residence certification — a framework that he notes has already been employed successfully by other states.
Gerber had entered the Resolutions Living facility in Santa Monica the night before his death, police said. It’s unclear whether he was already an outpatient receiving medical care at Resolutions Therapeutic Services or entirely new to the couple’s programs.

articles.title_orig: Republicans jump ship as Trump's anchor weighs heavy on party
articles.title_zh: Republicans jump ship as Trump's anchor weighs heavy on party
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Republican candidates facing increasingly dire prospects in the midterm election are starting to stiff-arm their unpopular standard-bearer, breaking with President Donald Trump as he threatens to drag down the party.
In Florida, Trump-endorsed Republican nominee for governor Byron Donalds wiped prominent mentions of the president from his website and Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar is criticizing the administration’s aggressive deportation push.
In two key Senate races, Republican candidates Ashley Hinson in Iowa and Mike Rogers in Michigan are calling for an end to the Iran war. And in historically Republican Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall is raising concerns about Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions in the state.
The growing GOP angst around running on Trump’s record comes as polls show most voters disapprove of the president and many of his core policies, including the U.S. war in Iran , sweeping tariffs on imports, and his hardline immigration crackdown .
Republican candidates have fallen behind Democrats in several key races that will decide control of Congress. Trump’s approval rating ‒ which sunk to a historic low of 32% in a Reuters/Ipsos poll this week ‒ is weighing on GOP candidates, who often are closely tied to the president and now face an electorate that takes a dim view of his performance.
“You’ve got to show that you’re different,” Republican pollster and Cygnal founder Brent Buchanan said of GOP candidates appealing to Trump voters who have soured on the president.
The Iran war and its economic fallout, particularly high gas prices , have put Republican congressional candidates in an especially difficult position as they navigate their allegiance to the president and voter dissatisfaction.
Trump has further complicated Republicans' midterm efforts by pushing controversial data centers that power artificial intelligence despite a nationwide backlash against the sprawling facilities, and angering ranchers in heavily Republican western states by working to expand imports of foreign beef to lower prices of the grocery staple.
Republican leaders have largely stood behind Trump as he pursed his aggressive second term agenda, offering little resistance in Congress or on the campaign trail. That wall of support is starting to crack amid signs that a potential blue wave is building, powered by opposition to Trump.
Yet GOP candidates could have a hard time distancing themselves from the president, who has been eager to make the election a referendum on his leadership, urging voters to "pretend" he’s on the ballot and pledging to be front and center on the campaign trail.
"This is way too little, way too late," said David Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron, arguing Republicans were "all for" making the midterms a referendum on Trump before his unpopularity in polls became clear. "These Republican candidates and elected officials are superglued to Trump, whether they want to be or not."
Taking the stage at the first-ever Republican midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month, Trump sought to rally his party around him ahead of the election. "On Nov. 3, the great American majority is going to stand up and continue to make America great again," Trump said.
Trump promised voters dividend checks of $5,000 if Republicans retain control of Congress, a proposal that was met with immediate skepticism among core MAGA allies and accusations of bribery from Democrats. He had supporters raise their hands, pledge their allegiance to him and promise to vote.
The event – dubbed "Trumpapalooza" by the Republican National Committee chair - was meant to project party unity and boost GOP voter enthusiasm, but even as Trump spoke there were signs within the arena of his party’s struggles.
Many seats were empty and some battleground candidates opted to skip the event.
Among them was Hinson, an Iowa Republican congresswoman who is trailing Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa's Senate race despite Trump carrying the state by double digits in 2024.
Hinson kept her distance in Dallas, attending a campaign fundraiser but not stepping foot on the convention stage where Trump gave primetime speeches both nights. She put more daylight between herself and the president this week when she called far an “immediate end” to the Iran war. She isn't the only GOP lawmaker speaking out on the war as Election Day nears.
Earlier this month, two other Iowa Republicans locked in tight races, Rep.  Zach Nunn and Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, backed a measure aimed at ending military operations in Iran.
Rogers, a former GOP congressman from Michigan and the state's Republican nominee for Senate , released an ad this week saying “the war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly.” Sen. John Husted, R-Ohio, made similar comments , as did Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany , the state's GOP candidate for governor.
"The president has final say in regards to this, but I just believe that we should be exiting Iran, that it's time to move on . . . time to come home, take care of business here in America," Tiffany said.
Tiffany and Hinson both voted repeatedly in Congress against directing Trump to stop the war, and Rogers has previously supported the president's efforts in Iran. The spike in fuel prices caused by the conflict has hit midwestern farm states particularly hard, though, and candidates there have been leading the rising GOP chorus to end the conflict.
With diesel prices at a record high and farmers feeling the pinch, Hinson, Rogers, Miller-Meeks and Alaska GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan all called this week for an embargo on selling the fuel abroad. Sullivan also skipped the convention as he faces a tough reelection campaign.
Buchanan said Republican candidates are struggling to win over Trump voters who are unhappy with the president's performance. His polling shows 12% of those who cast a ballot for the president are now wavering on voting for a Republican congressional candidate.
"That's why you're seeing these candidates break with Trump," said Buchanan, adding: "They've got to show that independent streak in order to pull as many of those 12% of voters back to them."
There are some signs Trump is starting to lose his grip on the Republican electorate.
A majority of Republican voters, 56%, in a poll from the opinion research firm Echelon Insights conducted last week said they consider themselves to be primarily a supporter of the Republican Party rather than a supporter of Trump. That compares to 59% who said they were more a supporter of Trump than the party when he took office for a second term in January 2025.
Yet Trump remains popular with his loyal MAGA base, creating a tough balancing act for GOP candidates. Hinson and Rogers didn't call out Trump directly in their statements, which don't mention the president.
"Republican candidates are in an extremely difficult position," said Nathan Gonzales, who runs the nonpartisan election handicapping firm Inside Elections. "If they try to distinguish themselves from President Trump in an effort to appeal to independent voters, they risk angering or alienating Republican voters who they also need to win."
In response to some Republicans breaking from Trump, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said the president remains the "unequivocal leader" and best messenger for Republicans.
"The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction," Ingle said.
Trump's approval rating has dropped amid the war ‒ which he said would last a few weeks and is now nearing the seven-month mark ‒ and high gas prices triggered by the conflict .
Just 39% of voters approve of the president's performance in the Real Clear Politics average of recent polls, down from 43% at the start of the war and 50% when he took office last year.

articles.title_orig: Europe frets as the Kremlin pushes the limits of its hybrid warfare
articles.title_zh: Europe frets as the Kremlin pushes the limits of its hybrid warfare
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin is testing Europe ‘s limits.
After months of covert attacks and sabotage across the continent, leaders are warning that Moscow may be about to grow bolder as it seeks to sow chaos and intimidate allies of Ukraine .
Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve to defend members on its eastern flank or respond to attacks that fall short of all-out war, these officials say, at a time when the U.S. is distracted by other conflicts and weighing reducing its military presence in Europe.
An assessment by the Danish Defence Intelligence Service released Thursday warned that in the coming months Moscow will further intensify its campaign of so-called hybrid warfare , “with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past.” It also assessed “a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia.”
While Moscow has for years embraced tactics that straddle the threshold of war, a string of increasingly brazen incidents in recent months has alarmed U.S. allies.
A key moment was the discovery of a Russian drone carrying explosives at an airport in eastern Germany near a Ukrainian aircraft last month. Berlin formally blamed Russia for what it said was a thwarted attack and imposed a diplomatic freeze, though Moscow denied involvement.
That incident appears to have changed the mindset about Russia’s growing threat in Europe, said Ed Arnold, a senior associate fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It just showed that Putin’s risk calculations are getting more liberal,” Arnold said. “Everyone just got a bit freaked out by that, quite frankly.”
It was followed by the unexpected visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow, during which NATO was discussed.
Incidents have continued to pile up — at defense facilities in Estonia, rail networks in Poland and the power grid in Germany. Many have passed without clear attribution, only intensifying speculation.
All this against the backdrop of near-daily drone incursions into European airspace, fueling anxiety in eastern border towns.
In Ukraine, a passenger train was hit less than 2 miles from the Polish border earlier this month, a close call on NATO’s doorstep that came as European diplomats returned from Kyiv on the same rail line. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at the station when the drone struck.
Just days later, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered the airspace of Lithuania, one of the Baltic member states whose proximity to Russia, analysts say, could make it a prime target for the Kremlin’s next move.
What could this look like? As unease increasingly swirled last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the Kremlin plans to launch drone and missile attacks against European countries that it would argue were accidental to try to weaken any response.
Russia has not claimed involvement in any of the incidents and has repeatedly denied conducting hybrid warfare or sabotage operations in NATO territory. Putin himself accused European leaders earlier this month of seeking out “a war against Russia” and “frightening their populations with an imaginary threat.”
On Friday, Russian state news agency RIA published and quickly deleted an op-ed laying out a potential scenario for a “lightning fast” war that Russia might wage against a NATO state, specifically focusing on the Baltic nations. The article was deleted because it did not “align” with editorial policy or Russia’s state policy, RIA said.
U.S. allies have little doubt that the broad pattern reflects the Kremlin increasingly pushing the boundaries.
“With these incidents now so frequent and so brazen, it is increasingly difficult to distinguish them from actual acts of war,” said Katja Bego, a senior research fellow with the Europe program at London-based think tank Chatham House. “The Kremlin is playing with fire here: The risk of more serious escalation — even if unintended — is very real.”
There is a mounting sense that something must be done, but what?
Lithuania has made plans for the evacuation of older adults and is lifting its ban on hosting nuclear weapons. Finland has warned citizens to be “mentally prepared” for new sabotage attacks. France is putting a plan in place to protect the country’s critical infrastructure.
Hanging over all of this is Article 5, NATO’s collective defense clause.
For Moscow, escalating hybrid attacks could highlight Western divisions over how best to respond and undermine the alliance at a time when the U.S. commitment to this mutual defense has been in question.
“I think they are trying to show Europe they can act without consequences, and more recently, to show Europe that the U.S. will not come to their rescue. It’s worrisome,” said William Alberque, a former senior NATO official based in Berlin.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Wednesday and told a media briefing that the U.S. was concerned that the Ukraine war could “metastasize and spread into other places ... be it through a hybrid attack, be it through a sabotage attack, be it through a misunderstanding.”
He added: “We watch reports carefully, and we raise them with the right people at the right levels.”
A State Department spokesperson told NBC News: “We continue to monitor Russia’s hybrid activities in Europe and are working closely with our allies and partners to strengthen resilience against the hybrid threat.”
Despite the spreading sense of alarm, some in Europe are urging against getting carried away.
NATO’s Baltic member states have not changed their security assessments, saying there is no imminent risk of a Russian invasion while much of Moscow’s military resources are tied up in Ukraine — and struggling to make progress there .
Latvia and Estonia directly border Russia, while Lithuania borders the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad. All three have been staunch supporters of Ukraine’s fight, driven in part by fears they could be next.
“Incursion of the type of 2022 Ukraine is not likely, let’s put it in a mild way,” Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs told reporters on the sidelines of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York. “Ukraine is fighting. Russia is absorbed in Ukraine. We do not observe any build-up near our borders,” Rinkēvičs added.
Neighboring Lithuania said this week a new rotation of U.S. troops was on its way to the country, ending uncertainty over a renewed deployment as the Pentagon weighs a broader plan to draw down U.S. forces on the continent.
“Russia’s pressure on Lithuania and other countries is not new,” Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas told NBC News, pointing to the decadelong Soviet occupation and adding that his country has more recently faced cyberattacks, disinformation and other forms of hostile influence from Moscow.
“There is no conventional threat at the moment,” Kaunas said via email, when asked why his country has not changed its security assessment. “At the same time, provocations and false-flag operations remain possible, and our intelligence points to increasingly aggressive Russian behavior. These are different threats, and they need different answers.”
But failing to take sufficient action could carry its own risks.
“Respond. Always respond,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged his European allies earlier this week.
“If you don’t respond to Russians, they will go further.”
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.title_zh: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.content_orig:
A year ago, Meta was struggling to convince Silicon Valley that it could keep up in the AI race. Now it has one of the industry's hottest products.
Muse, Meta's new personal AI assistant, has rocketed to the top of the App Store and become a victory lap for CEO Mark Zuckerberg's massive AI spending. Meta's Connect conference this week was all about the app, which AI chief Alexandr Wang — who is 29 and has been posting risqué memes of Muse's mascot all week — called a "banger."
Getting there required months of painstaking work, a team led by former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, and thousands of employees pulled from across Meta to teach the agent how to actually get things done, employees told Business Insider.
Meta also snapped up top AI agent talent through acqui-hires, including the leaders of Dreamer, an AI agent startup.
Whether Meta can sustain Muse's momentum is another question. Competitors like Instinct are thriving, and OpenAI is widely expected to launch a rival. Privacy concerns have also arisen, as Muse requires broad access to users' accounts to function. Meta employees are still reeling from a year of mass layoffs, employee surveillance, and low morale.
For now, at least, Muse's success — and a more than 20% increase in Meta's stock price since its launch — has become a morale boost, employees said. It also proves that Meta remains firmly in the AI race after being seen as a laggard a year ago.
"Muse is busy working for millions of people because of the hard work of a bunch of people at Meta — and we're still cooking," a Meta spokesperson said.
Muse's success was far from inevitable.
Since September 2025, Friedman, who heads the superintelligence unit's Products and Applied Research team , has been working hard on Muse, then codenamed "Hatch."
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
As recently as two weeks before Muse's launch this month, the chatbot struggled with speaking good English, a person directly familiar with the matter said — and it came as a huge relief when it finally started scoring well on coherence tests.
Earlier this year, some of Meta's top AI employees were also worried about Muse, an employee told Business Insider. They had tried it out and found it working poorly — it felt like just another chatbot, but with a worse underlying AI model and extra steps, that person added.
Friedman's team eventually pulled it off. Tens of thousands of Meta employees tested Muse for months, coming up with a range of use cases for the agent, which became key to the effort.
That data helped Friedman's team improve Muse's ability to do things like book meetings and cancel plane tickets: the painful work of getting better at increasingly complex tasks, or "hill-climbing," as Silicon Valley calls it.
The team trained Muse to be considerate so that it didn't overshare, like telling people someone couldn't make a meeting because they were hungover, the person familiar said. Meta also focused on ensuring it could interact with the internet seamlessly by using tools it hadn't used before.
"Our researchers did a ton of work teaching agents how to choose the right tool for a job," Wang said this week at Connect.
Friedman's role was critical. Zuckerberg brought in the executive last year as part of a deal to buy a stake in his venture capital fund, NFDG. Last year, Friedman and Wang cowrote a memo outlining a "superintelligent personal sidekick" that would act as a trusted friend and advisor.
Friedman is unabashedly technical and hands-on. Internally, the executive is opinionated and proud of it, chafing with other teams across Meta's sprawling operations, one of the employees said. Meta's communications chief, Andy Stone, recently called him "Nat the Truthteller" after he derided a report about Muse's security as written by "dummies."
He also moves fast. His bare-bones personal website spells out his philosophy in characteristically blunt terms: "slow is fake" and "it's important to do things fast," it says. Friedman has pushed Meta's AI staff to ditch slow internal tools in favor of faster external ones, such as Vercel.
When the independent AI agent OpenClaw took the tech world by storm this winter, Friedman acted quickly. The free desktop-based tool was popular with developers, but mystifying to everyday users. Friedman aimed to build a far more accessible version from scratch.
He issued a two-page internal memo titled "The Claw Is The Law," praising the product, and also bought hundreds of Mac Minis for Meta's superintelligence team to run the agent.
While Muse is user-friendly now, making it all happen took "months of blood, sweat, and tears," the person familiar said.
Although it took a "long ass time," now it's something that anyone's "grandma can use," Wang later posted.
Meta also went on a hiring binge for researchers and engineers in agentic AI. It hired David Singleton and Hugo Barra, the cofounders of Dreamer, a startup helping people build their own agents, along with the rest of their team.
Singleton has worked on Muse since he began at Meta in March, helping design the core technology that enables the app to store sensitive information securely, he posted on X.
The efforts worked. Although the arrival of the viral AI agent Instinct initially upstaged Meta , Muse took off by tapping into Meta's enormous built-in audience across its apps — including among people who had never used AI agents before.
Meta wasn't the only one on a hiring spree. OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator , Pete Steinberger, in a coup earlier this year. Meta was especially worried that it would be upstaged by a large competitor, the person familiar with the matter said, and the team was shocked as the months went by without such an entrant.
Wall Street is cheering on Muse, seeing it as a way for Meta to become more than an ad company. Zuckerberg told Alex Heath's Sources earlier this month that he wants people to shop and save money on Muse, which Meta plans to make money from by taking a small cut of each transaction.
"We see the Meta bull case increasingly playing out," Mizuho Americas analyst Lloyd Walmsley wrote in a note.
Users have praised how easy it is to set up Muse. Hadi Javeed, the cofounder of healthcare startup RevelAi, said his dad saw an ad for Muse in his Facebook feed and downloaded it, promptly using it to buy a new pair of shoes.
"They completely deleted all the setup that was required," Javeed said.
At the same time, Javeed, like many others, has raised data privacy concerns about Muse. By design, an app like Muse creates a new order of security and privacy risks, such as the app buying things without a user's permission. Privacy and trust remain key roadblocks to broader adoption of Muse, Bank of America analysts wrote.
Zuckerberg has said that the company held back Muse's launch due to safety and product liability concerns. He and Friedman also personally reached out to Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to help co-design Muse's security architecture, Zuckerberg told Heath.
For now, Meta is on a high. The company has hinted that much more will come as it works on a new AI model, Watermelon. It says the model has already caught up with OpenAI. Wang says Meta has other ideas that are "just as big" as Muse.
"The kitchen is just getting warmed up," he posted on X.
